units.title: Fundamentals
units.tip: Machine learning is about building models that learn patterns from data. Every dataset has features (inputs) and labels (outputs). A good model generalizes from training data to unseen data.

exercises.question: What is a 'feature' in machine learning?
exercises.answer: An input variable that the model uses to make predictions
exercises.explain: A feature is an observable property of the data. In predicting house prices, features might be square footage, location, and year built.
choices: An input variable that the model uses to make predictions
The correct answer for a prediction
A property of the neural network

exercises.question: What is a 'label'?
exercises.answer: The output or target value that the model learns to predict
exercises.explain: A label is the ground truth. To predict house prices, the label is the actual price. Features predict the label.
choices: The output or target value that the model learns to predict

exercises.question: What is 'supervised learning'?
exercises.answer: Learning from labeled data where each example has a known target output
exercises.explain: In supervised learning, you have pairs of (features, label). The model learns to map features to labels. Classification and regression are supervised learning tasks.
choices: Learning from labeled data where each example has a known target output
A human teaching the model step by step

exercises.question: What is 'unsupervised learning'?
exercises.answer: Learning patterns from data without labels, finding structure in the data
exercises.explain: In unsupervised learning, data has no labels. The model finds patterns, clusters, or representations. Clustering is a common unsupervised task.
choices: Learning patterns from data without labels, finding structure in the data

exercises.question: What is an 'observation' or 'example' in a dataset?
exercises.answer: A single row of data with feature values and a label
exercises.explain: An observation is one data point. A dataset of house prices has many observations, each with square footage, location, and price.
choices: A single row of data with feature values and a label

exercises.question: What is the 'training set'?
exercises.answer: Data used to fit the model and learn its parameters
exercises.explain: The training set is given to the learning algorithm. The model learns patterns in this data. Typical split is 70-80% of data for training.
choices: Data the model has never seen
Data used to evaluate the final model
Data used to fit the model and learn its parameters

exercises.question: What is the 'validation set'?
exercises.answer: Data used to tune hyperparameters and select the best model during training
exercises.explain: The validation set is used to evaluate model performance while training. You can use it to pick hyperparameters or choose which model variant to use.
choices: Data that is never seen by the model
Data used to tune hyperparameters and select the best model during training

exercises.question: What is the 'test set'?
exercises.answer: Data held out until the end to evaluate final model performance
exercises.explain: The test set is unseen during development. You evaluate your final model on the test set to get a realistic estimate of performance on new data.
choices: Data held out until the end to evaluate final model performance
Data used to train the model

exercises.question: Why is it important to split data into train/validation/test?
exercises.answer: To evaluate how well the model generalizes to unseen data
exercises.explain: If you evaluate the model on training data, it will always look great but may be overfitting. Test data gives an honest estimate of real-world performance.
choices: To evaluate how well the model generalizes to unseen data

exercises.question: What is a 'hyperparameter'?
exercises.answer: A setting of the learning algorithm that is not learned from data but chosen before training
exercises.explain: Examples: learning rate, number of trees in a forest, k in k-nearest neighbors. These are not learned; you set them before training and often tune them on the validation set.
choices: A setting of the learning algorithm that is not learned from data but chosen before training

units.title: Regression
units.tip: Regression predicts continuous values. A model learns a function that maps inputs to outputs. Linear regression is the simplest case but extensions handle non-linear relationships.

exercises.question: What is 'regression'?
exercises.answer: Predicting a continuous numerical output from input features
exercises.explain: Regression outputs a real number, not a category. Predicting house prices, temperature, or stock values are regression tasks.
choices: Predicting a continuous numerical output from input features
Reducing the size of a dataset

exercises.question: What is 'linear regression'?
exercises.answer: Fitting a line (or hyperplane) to data to predict continuous values
exercises.explain: Linear regression assumes a linear relationship: y = mx + b. It finds the best line that fits the training data. Simple but effective.
choices: Drawing a line on a graph
Fitting a line (or hyperplane) to data to predict continuous values

exercises.question: What is the 'slope' in a linear regression model y = mx + b?
exercises.answer: The coefficient m that determines how much y changes when x increases
exercises.explain: The slope m is the learned parameter. If m = 2, then y increases by 2 for every 1 unit increase in x.
choices: The coefficient m that determines how much y changes when x increases

exercises.question: What is the 'intercept' or 'bias' in y = mx + b?
exercises.answer: The constant b that is added to the prediction regardless of inputs
exercises.explain: The intercept b is the value of y when x = 0. It shifts the line up or down.
choices: The constant b that is added to the prediction regardless of inputs

exercises.question: How does linear regression find the best line?
exercises.answer: By minimizing the sum of squared differences between predicted and actual values
exercises.explain: Linear regression finds parameters (m and b) that minimize squared error. This is called least squares fitting.
choices: By minimizing the sum of squared differences between predicted and actual values

exercises.question: What is 'classification'?
exercises.answer: Predicting a category or class label for an input
exercises.explain: Classification outputs a discrete label, not a number. Spam vs. not-spam, cat vs. dog, or high/medium/low risk are classification problems.
choices: Predicting a category or class label for an input

exercises.question: What is 'logistic regression'?
exercises.answer: A regression method adapted for binary classification by predicting probabilities
exercises.explain: Logistic regression outputs a probability (0 to 1) for the positive class. It uses a logistic function to squash linear predictions into the range [0, 1].
choices: A regression method adapted for binary classification by predicting probabilities
A linear regression with no intercept

exercises.question: What is the 'sigmoid function' in logistic regression?
exercises.answer: A mathematical function that maps any input to a probability between 0 and 1
exercises.explain: The sigmoid function is S-shaped. It converts linear predictions to probabilities. It is defined as 1 / (1 + e^(-z)) where z is the linear prediction.
choices: A mathematical function that maps any input to a probability between 0 and 1

exercises.question: What is 'non-linear regression'?
exercises.answer: Fitting a curve (not a line) to data to model non-linear relationships
exercises.explain: Real data often has non-linear patterns. Non-linear regression uses polynomials, splines, or other curves. Example: y = ax^2 + bx + c.
choices: Fitting a curve (not a line) to data to model non-linear relationships

exercises.question: What is 'polynomial regression'?
exercises.answer: Using polynomial features (x, x^2, x^3) to fit non-linear relationships
exercises.explain: Polynomial regression treats x^2, x^3, etc. as features and applies linear regression. Example: y = a + bx + cx^2 fits a parabola.
choices: Using polynomial features (x, x^2, x^3) to fit non-linear relationships
Using polynomials in the feature names

units.title: Decision Trees and Neighbors
units.tip: Decision trees partition feature space by asking yes/no questions. K-nearest neighbors classifies by looking at nearby examples. Both are intuitive and powerful.

exercises.question: What is a 'decision tree'?
exercises.answer: A tree-like model that partitions data using a sequence of if-then rules
exercises.explain: A decision tree asks questions like 'Is age > 30?' If yes, go left; if no, go right. Each question splits the data until you reach a leaf with a prediction.
choices: A tree-like model that partitions data using a sequence of if-then rules

exercises.question: What is a 'split' or 'node' in a decision tree?
exercises.answer: A question that divides data based on a feature and threshold
exercises.explain: At each node, the tree selects a feature and a threshold. Data is split into two groups based on whether the feature exceeds the threshold.
choices: A question that divides data based on a feature and threshold

exercises.question: What is a 'leaf' in a decision tree?
exercises.answer: A final node that outputs a prediction without further splits
exercises.explain: A leaf is the end of a path through the tree. It contains the prediction: the most common class (classification) or average value (regression).
choices: A final node that outputs a prediction without further splits

exercises.question: What is 'tree depth'?
exercises.answer: The number of questions (splits) on the longest path from root to leaf
exercises.explain: Deeper trees can learn complex patterns but tend to overfit. Shallow trees are simpler but may underfit.
choices: The number of questions (splits) on the longest path from root to leaf

exercises.question: Why do deep decision trees tend to overfit?
exercises.answer: They ask many questions, fitting noise and details specific to training data
exercises.explain: A very deep tree can memorize the training data, learning quirks that do not generalize. Limiting tree depth prevents overfitting.
choices: Deep trees only work on small datasets
They ask many questions, fitting noise and details specific to training data
Depth causes the model to forget

exercises.question: What is 'k-nearest neighbors' (kNN)?
exercises.answer: Classifying by finding the k closest examples in the training set and using their labels
exercises.explain: kNN is lazy: it stores all training data. To classify a new point, it finds the k nearest neighbors and votes. The prediction is the majority class.
choices: Classifying by finding the k closest examples in the training set and using their labels

exercises.question: What does 'k' mean in k-nearest neighbors?
exercises.answer: The number of nearest neighbors to consider when making a prediction
exercises.explain: With k=3, you look at the 3 closest examples. With k=1, you look at the single closest example. Larger k reduces noise but may miss fine details.
choices: The number of nearest neighbors to consider when making a prediction

exercises.question: How does kNN measure 'distance' between examples?
exercises.answer: Using a metric like Euclidean distance: distance = sqrt((x1-x2)^2 + (y1-y2)^2)
exercises.explain: Euclidean distance is the most common. Other metrics exist: Manhattan distance, cosine distance, etc. The choice affects which neighbors are considered nearest.
choices: Using a metric like Euclidean distance: distance = sqrt((x1-x2)^2 + (y1-y2)^2)

exercises.question: Why is kNN called 'lazy learning'?
exercises.answer: It does no training; it only stores data and computes predictions at query time
exercises.explain: kNN has no explicit training phase. When you query, it searches the stored training data. This delays computation until prediction time.
choices: It does no training; it only stores data and computes predictions at query time

exercises.question: What is a problem with kNN on large datasets?
exercises.answer: Storing and searching large amounts of data is slow at prediction time
exercises.explain: kNN needs to compute distances to all training examples. With millions of examples, this is expensive. It also uses a lot of memory.
choices: Storing and searching large amounts of data is slow at prediction time

units.title: Unsupervised Learning
units.tip: Unsupervised learning finds structure in data without labels. Clustering groups similar examples together. K-means is a simple and popular clustering algorithm.

exercises.question: What is 'clustering'?
exercises.answer: Grouping similar examples together without using labels
exercises.explain: Clustering discovers natural groups in data. It is unsupervised: you do not tell the model which group each example belongs to.
choices: Grouping similar examples together without using labels

exercises.question: What is a 'cluster'?
exercises.answer: A group of similar examples that the model assigns together
exercises.explain: A cluster contains examples that are close in feature space. Examples in the same cluster are similar; examples in different clusters are dissimilar.
choices: A group of similar examples that the model assigns together

exercises.question: What is a 'centroid' in clustering?
exercises.answer: The center point of a cluster, representing the average position of all examples in the cluster
exercises.explain: A centroid is like a representative of the cluster. For a cluster of customers, the centroid is the average customer in that group.
choices: The largest example in a cluster
The center point of a cluster, representing the average position of all examples in the cluster
The first example in a cluster

exercises.question: How many clusters should you use?
exercises.answer: That depends on the data and the application; you may need to experiment
exercises.explain: There is no single correct answer. You can use methods like the elbow method to find a good number of clusters, but ultimately it depends on your goal.
choices: That depends on the data and the application; you may need to experiment

exercises.question: What is the 'elbow method'?
exercises.answer: Plotting cluster quality against number of clusters and finding where it levels off
exercises.explain: As you increase clusters, quality improves. At some point, adding more clusters helps less. The elbow (the bend) suggests a good number of clusters.
choices: Plotting cluster quality against number of clusters and finding where it levels off
Using your elbow to press the mouse
A type of joint in the data

exercises.question: What is 'k-means clustering'?
exercises.answer: An algorithm that partitions data into k clusters by iteratively updating centroids
exercises.explain: K-means initializes k centroids, assigns examples to the nearest centroid, then updates centroids as the mean of assigned examples. It repeats until convergence.
choices: A regression algorithm with k features
An algorithm that partitions data into k clusters by iteratively updating centroids
A classifier that uses k neighbors
A decision tree with k leaves

exercises.question: What are the main steps of k-means?
exercises.answer: Initialize centroids, assign examples to nearest centroid, update centroids, repeat
exercises.explain: K-means alternates between assigning and updating until centroids stop moving. No iteration increases the total within-cluster distance.
choices: Initialize centroids, assign examples to nearest centroid, update centroids, repeat

exercises.question: What is the 'objective' or 'loss' that k-means minimizes?
exercises.answer: The sum of squared distances from each example to its assigned centroid
exercises.explain: K-means minimizes within-cluster variance: sum of squared distances from examples to their cluster centers. Tighter clusters have lower loss.
choices: The sum of squared distances from each example to its assigned centroid
The size of the largest cluster

exercises.question: Why does k-means not always find the global optimum?
exercises.answer: Initialization and local minima: different starting centroids may lead to different results
exercises.explain: K-means is greedy and can get stuck in local minima. Running it multiple times with different initializations helps find better solutions.
choices: The data has no global optimum
It always finds the optimal solution
Initialization and local minima: different starting centroids may lead to different results

exercises.question: What is a limitation of k-means?
exercises.answer: It assumes clusters are roughly spherical and similarly sized
exercises.explain: K-means works well for round clusters of similar size. It struggles with elongated or very differently sized clusters.
choices: It assumes clusters are roughly spherical and similarly sized

units.title: Model Evaluation
units.tip: Evaluating a model tells you how well it works. Different metrics suit different tasks. Accuracy is simple but can be misleading with imbalanced data.

exercises.question: What is 'accuracy'?
exercises.answer: The fraction of correct predictions out of all predictions
exercises.explain: Accuracy = (correct predictions) / (total predictions). With 100 examples and 90 correct, accuracy is 0.90 or 90%.
choices: The fraction of correct predictions out of all predictions

exercises.question: What is a 'confusion matrix'?
exercises.answer: A table showing true positives, true negatives, false positives, and false negatives
exercises.explain: A confusion matrix breaks down predictions into four categories: correct yes, correct no, wrong yes, wrong no. It reveals what types of mistakes the model makes.
choices: A matrix that confuses the model
A table showing true positives, true negatives, false positives, and false negatives

exercises.question: What is 'precision'?
exercises.answer: Of the examples predicted positive, how many were actually positive
exercises.explain: Precision = TP / (TP + FP). It answers: when the model says yes, how often is it right? Precision matters when false positives are costly.
choices: Of the examples predicted positive, how many were actually positive
Of the positive examples, how many did the model find
The total number of correct predictions

exercises.question: What is 'recall' or 'sensitivity'?
exercises.answer: Of the actual positive examples, how many did the model correctly identify
exercises.explain: Recall = TP / (TP + FN). It answers: of all actual positives, how many did the model find? Recall matters when missing positives is costly (e.g., disease detection).
choices: Of the actual positive examples, how many did the model correctly identify

exercises.question: What is the 'F1 score'?
exercises.answer: The harmonic mean of precision and recall, balancing both metrics
exercises.explain: F1 = 2 * (precision * recall) / (precision + recall). It is useful when you care about both false positives and false negatives.
choices: The sum of precision and recall
The harmonic mean of precision and recall, balancing both metrics

exercises.question: In the bias-variance trade-off, what does 'bias' mean?
exercises.answer: The error from a model being too simple and unable to capture true patterns
exercises.explain: High bias means the model oversimplifies. A straight line fitting curved data has high bias. It underfits.
choices: The difference between prediction and truth
The error from a model being too simple and unable to capture true patterns
The intercept term in a model
A preference for one class over another

exercises.question: What is 'variance' in machine learning?
exercises.answer: The error from a model being too complex and fitting noise in the data
exercises.explain: High variance means the model is sensitive to small changes in training data. It fits quirks and noise. It overfits.
choices: The number of features in the model
The error from a model being too complex and fitting noise in the data

exercises.question: What is the 'bias-variance trade-off'?
exercises.answer: As you reduce bias, variance increases, and vice versa; the goal is to balance both
exercises.explain: A simple model has high bias but low variance. A complex model has low bias but high variance. The best model balances these two sources of error.
choices: One is always more important than the other
As you reduce bias, variance increases, and vice versa; the goal is to balance both

exercises.question: What is 'regularization'?
exercises.answer: A technique that penalizes complex models to reduce overfitting
exercises.explain: Regularization adds a penalty term for model complexity. Larger weights are penalized, discouraging the model from fitting noise.
choices: A technique that penalizes complex models to reduce overfitting
Scaling every feature to the same range

exercises.question: What is 'L2 regularization' or 'ridge regression'?
exercises.answer: Penalizing the sum of squared weights to prevent large weights
exercises.explain: L2 adds a term proportional to the sum of squared weights to the loss. It shrinks weights but rarely makes them exactly zero.
choices: Penalizing the sum of squared weights to prevent large weights
Penalizing the sum of absolute weights
Requiring all weights to be equal

units.title: Advanced Metrics and Concepts
units.tip: Beyond accuracy, many metrics help evaluate models fairly. ROC curves, precision-recall curves, and other tools reveal performance trade-offs. Cross-validation gives robust error estimates.

exercises.question: What is an 'ROC curve'?
exercises.answer: A curve showing the trade-off between true positive rate and false positive rate
exercises.explain: ROC (Receiver Operating Characteristic) plots TPR vs. FPR as the classification threshold changes. A curve closer to the top-left is better.
choices: A curve showing the trade-off between true positive rate and false positive rate
A graph of predictions over time

exercises.question: What is 'AUC' (Area Under the Curve)?
exercises.answer: The area under the ROC curve, a single number summarizing model performance
exercises.explain: AUC ranges from 0 to 1. AUC = 0.5 means random guessing. AUC = 1 means perfect classification. Higher is better.
choices: The area under the ROC curve, a single number summarizing model performance
The area under a decision boundary

exercises.question: What is a 'precision-recall curve'?
exercises.answer: A curve showing the trade-off between precision and recall as the classification threshold changes
exercises.explain: Like ROC, but for precision and recall. Useful when classes are imbalanced. A curve in the top-right corner is best.
choices: A curve showing the trade-off between precision and recall as the classification threshold changes

exercises.question: What is a 'threshold' in classification?
exercises.answer: The probability cutoff: predictions above it are positive, below are negative
exercises.explain: By default, the threshold is 0.5. Lowering it makes the model more likely to predict positive (higher recall, lower precision). Raising it does the opposite.
choices: The probability cutoff: predictions above it are positive, below are negative

exercises.question: When should you use a non-0.5 threshold?
exercises.answer: When the costs of false positives and false negatives are different
exercises.explain: If missing a cancer diagnosis (false negative) is much worse than a false alarm (false positive), lower the threshold.
choices: When the costs of false positives and false negatives are different

exercises.question: What is 'cross-validation'?
exercises.answer: A technique that splits data into folds and repeatedly trains and evaluates on different splits
exercises.explain: Cross-validation uses the data more efficiently than a single train/test split. With k-fold CV, you split into k folds, train k times using different test sets, and average results.
choices: A technique that splits data into folds and repeatedly trains and evaluates on different splits

exercises.question: What is 'k-fold cross-validation'?
exercises.answer: Splitting data into k folds, training k models leaving one fold out, and averaging the results
exercises.explain: With 5-fold CV, split data into 5 equal parts. Train 5 models, each leaving one fold for testing. Final score is the average.
choices: Training k models on the same data
Splitting data into k folds, training k models leaving one fold out, and averaging the results

exercises.question: What is 'overfitting'?
exercises.answer: A model that learns training data too well, fitting noise, and fails on new data
exercises.explain: An overfit model has low training error but high test error. It memorizes rather than generalizes. Signs: training accuracy very high but test accuracy drops.
choices: A model that learns training data too well, fitting noise, and fails on new data

exercises.question: What is 'underfitting'?
exercises.answer: A model that is too simple and fails to learn patterns in the data
exercises.explain: An underfit model has high error on both training and test data. It is not complex enough. Signs: both accuracies low.
choices: Training on a dataset that is too large
A model that is too simple and fails to learn patterns in the data

exercises.question: How do you detect overfitting?
exercises.answer: Compare training and test error: if test error is much higher, the model is overfitting
exercises.explain: Training error may be low. If test error is high, the model overfit. A learning curve showing diverging training and test errors is a sign.
choices: Compare training and test error: if test error is much higher, the model is overfitting
